sentences: Beneath the night sky, snow-covered mountains tower over everything.
This is a cold, blue world of winter.
The painting is Winter Night in the Mountains, by the Norwegian painter Harald Sohlberg.
It was painted in oil on canvas in 1914, and it is a large picture, 160.4 centimetres high and 180 centimetres wide.
It belongs to the Nasjonalmuseet, Norway's National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design, in Oslo.
Look first at the mountains.
These are the Rondane mountains in central Norway.
The museum compares Sohlberg's peaks to a snow-covered palace, and indeed they glow like walls of ice.
There is no sign of a human being anywhere.
Now look up at the sky.
In the murky darkness, a few stars can just be glimpsed.
The white glow of the snow meets the deep blue of the night, and the whole picture settles into stillness.
Look at the trees in the foreground.
Bare trees and bushes, stripped of every leaf, stand as dark silhouettes, gathered on each side almost like a stage curtain.
Between them, our eyes are drawn deep into the distant winter mountains.
Sohlberg insisted that this foreground must not look too dense or too wild.
It was there, he wrote, that the night and the anxiety of the picture should live.
Within this beautiful view, he hid a feeling of unease.
The picture began on an Easter skiing trip in 1899.
Sohlberg made his first sketch on the train home, and for the next fifteen years he returned to Rondane again and again.
He took photographs to study the mountains, and he produced several paintings, many drawings and a popular print of the motif.
This is the largest and final version of them all.
It was first shown in 1914 at the jubilee exhibition marking the hundredth anniversary of the Norwegian Constitution.
The following year a collector bought it, and in 1918 he gave it to the National Gallery.
Sohlberg was born in 1869 and died in 1935.

In 1995, in a public vote run by the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation, this painting was chosen as Norway's national painting, and today a lookout point named after him, Sohlbergplassen, stands by Lake Atnsjøen as a stop on one of Norway's National Tourist Routes.
Step back and take it in once more.
This single night is what remained after fifteen years of looking at the same mountains.
Think of a place you have carried in your heart for a long time and would like to visit again.
